title: Settings That Change While Running: Typed Parameters, Validation and Changing Several at Once

questions.question: Why must a set of a name that was never declared be refused?
options: Undeclared names are slower to look up than declared ones
A new setting would have no type, and every setting needs one
Because two nodes might then create the same name
A mistyped name would create a setting the node never reads, and the operator would believe it had changed something
questions.explanation: The node only reads the settings it declared. Accepting ki when the node reads kp would report success for a change that did nothing.

questions.question: A parameter is declared as a real. A client sets it to the integer 5. What happens?
options: It is refused: wrong type, because 1 is not 1.0 and a silent conversion hides which side was wrong
It is converted to 5.0 and accepted, since no information is lost
It is accepted and the parameter becomes an integer from then on
It is accepted with a warning in the log
questions.explanation: A setting's type is fixed when it is declared. Converting quietly would hide the fact that one side has the wrong idea of what the setting is.

questions.question: kp is limited to 0 to 100. Which of these is accepted?
options: Only values strictly between 0 and 100, so neither end was accepted
0 and 100, the ends of the range, while 250 and -1 were refused as out of range
250, clamped down to 100
-1, clamped up to 0
questions.explanation: A range includes its limits. Outside it the set is refused and the gain stays as it was; nothing is clamped.

questions.question: Three changes are requested and the last has the wrong type. What state are the settings in afterwards?
options: The first two are applied and the third refused, so kp had changed and enabled had too
All three are applied, and the wrong typed one is converted
As they were: all or none, so kp was still 2.0 and enabled still true
None are applied and all three settings are reset to their defaults
questions.explanation: A client that changes three things means all three. Checking them on a copy and applying only if every one passes avoids running with half a change.

questions.question: min_speed 0.1 and max_speed 1.0 must become 2.0 and 3.0, with the rule min below max. What happens one at a time and together?
options: Both are refused: the rule compares each new value with the old one
One at a time the first step breaks the rule and is refused, and together the rule sees the end and passes
One at a time works, and together is refused because two changes conflict
Both work: the rule is only checked when the node restarts
questions.explanation: Raising the minimum to 2.0 while the maximum is still 1.0 breaks the rule on the way. Asked for together, only the end state is judged.

questions.question: What does a read only setting protect against?
options: A value outside its range, such as a gain of 250
A value of the wrong type, such as an integer for a real
A change from outside to something that must not change while running, such as a serial number: the set was refused and the value stayed A-1001
A name that was never declared
questions.explanation: Some settings describe the node and are not controls. Declared read only, a set from outside is refused and the value is unchanged.
